In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV‐infected kidney and liver transplant recipients on IS require close monitoring and dose modifications of both ARVs and IS to ensure optimal pharmacological and clinical outcomes.
the pharmacokinetics of CsA and FK are affected by the co‐administration of ARV drugs, particularly when the latter include PIs, but that the effect of NNRTIs is less clear.
the immunosuppressive drug dosages should be reduced when combined with protease inhibitor‐based antiretrovirus therapy and increased when combined with efavirenz‐based antiretoviral therapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in patients with HIV infection, the pharmacokinetics of the IS are significantly altered by the concomitant use with ARVs, and these alterations are more pronounced in those using PIs.
HIV‐infected kidney and liver transplant recipients on IS and ARVs require careful monitoring of IS concentrations and dose adjustments to avoid IS toxicity or insufficient immunosuppressive effects.
HIV‐infected solid organ transplant recipients on PIs or EFV with CsA, Sr or FK, require a reduction in IS dose or increase in IS dosing interval to maintain therapeutic drug concentrations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIV‐infected kidney or liver transplant recipients on IS and PIs or NNRTIs require close monitoring and dose adjustments to maintain therapeutic levels of immunosuppressive drugs.
HIV‐infected solid organ transplant recipients on PIs require lower IS doses than those on NNRTI‐based regimens.
the use of NNRTIs, especially EFV, with IS is associated with significant drug interactions that may lead to toxicity or suboptimal immunosuppression.
